claims.text: The initial refractory high-entropy alloy is a homogeneous, single-phase BCC solid solution produced by vacuum arc melting and contains no intentional oxide dispersion.
Approximately 2 at.% yttrium will be added during alloy synthesis.
Adding approximately 2 at.% yttrium and subsequently processing or annealing the alloy will induce in situ precipitation of Y2O3.
The intervention will produce a fine, uniform dispersion of nanoscale Y2O3 precipitates in the BCC matrix.
Y2O3 dispersoids will impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion will increase elevated-temperature yield strength.
Impeded dislocation motion will increase elevated-temperature tensile strength.
Y2O3 dispersoids will act as sinks for irradiation-induced defects.
The defect sinks will capture and annihilate irradiation-induced defects.
Defect capture and annihilation by the dispersoids will mitigate irradiation damage and preserve matrix integrity.
The Y2O3 dispersoids will resist undesirable coarsening during high-temperature and irradiation exposure.
The intervention will avoid undesirable phase transformations during high-temperature and irradiation exposure.
Relative to the Y-free baseline, the yttrium-modified alloy will exhibit approximately a 15% increase in elevated-temperature yield and tensile strength.
Relative to the Y-free baseline, the yttrium-modified alloy will retain mechanical properties better under irradiation.
The Y2O3 dispersoids will remain thermally stable and effective as defect sinks during service.
A conventional Y-free, single-phase BCC refractory HEA typically has lower high-temperature yield strength than the proposed Y-containing alloy.
A conventional Y-free, single-phase BCC refractory HEA typically undergoes more pronounced irradiation-induced microstructural degradation than the proposed Y-containing alloy.

The proposed benefits are expected from 800 to 1200 °C under irradiation doses relevant to nuclear or space applications, provided a uniform nanometric Y2O3 dispersion forms without deleterious phases or excessive embrittlement.
